aggregate.detectors_note: A detector's denominator (`answerable_for`) is the labelled flags it was answerable for: every flag it spoke on with no `blame` (§5.4's rule that whatever raised an unwanted flag shares the charge), plus the flags whose `blame` named it. A flag whose `blame` named other detectors is not charged here, and one blamed on `score` is in no detector's denominator at all — so these denominators do not sum to the corpus total, by design. `spoke` is the wider count (every flag at this cut whose findings included this detector's) and is shown so the narrow one reads as a share of it. A detector with `g3: null` raised nothing here, which is no evidence rather than a clean bill of health (ADR-001 §7.7); `defaults.never_fired` names them.

formulas.F(tau,W): risk(e) >= tau, or any finding at severity high
formulas.FP(e): a dismissal whose reason code is in `fp_reasons`
formulas.G3: |{e in F(tau,W): labelled(e) and FP(e)}| / |{e in F(tau,W): labelled(e)}| — ADR-001 §5.4
formulas.TP(e): disposition `accepted`, or rework(e) — see labelling_note. TP is reported beside G3 and is not in its denominator: §5.4's denominator is every labelled flag, true positives and false ones together
formulas.labelling_note: ADR-001 §5.4 names §5.4's four false-positive codes as `expected`, `not-applicable`, `low-stakes` and `false-positive`. The closed list that actually shipped is `e4.6`'s (`fathom_analyze::queue::REASONS`), and the mapping is a collapse, not an invention: §5.4's `expected` is shipped `intentional` ("what looks risky here is what I wanted"); §5.4's `low-stakes` and `false-positive` are shipped under their own names; §5.4's `not-applicable` has no separate shipped code — `false-positive`'s claim ("the finding that raised this does not describe my change") already covers the case, so the two measure together and this file says so instead of hiding the collapse. §5.4's true positive `accepted-with-required-change` is shipped `accepted`: `e4.6`'s ledger has no 'with required change' refinement, so a flag that earned a review that happened is the true positive, and rework of the episode counts as one too per §5.4's own `TP(e)` clause. The five shipped codes that are neither (`not-my-area`, `already-known`, `superseded`, `will-revert`, `other`) are dismissals about the reviewer's attention or the queue's state rather than about the flag: they sit in `G3`'s denominator exactly as §5.4 writes it — the reviewer looked, so the flag cost something — and never in its numerator.
formulas.mature: >= 5 successors on the lineage, or older than 7 days against the pin's clock
formulas.miss_rate: |{e in Mature(W): rework(e) and risk(e) < tau}| / |{e in Mature(W): rework(e)}|
formulas.rework: ADR-001 §5.3 R1|R2|R3 with N = 5; R1's content rung fires at an undo share >= 0.90
formulas.tau_note: §5.4 tightens the *rate* at 1.0 (0.15), not the threshold: tau stays 70 in both gates, so the two `g3-*` gates are one flag set read against two bars. If a later release tunes tau, it changes here, in the document, and the harness's own check against the shipped `risk.tau` is what catches a copy that drifted.

gates.claim: at §5.4's published default tau the aggregate false-positive rate clears the alpha gate — measured: six episodes out of 540 reached tau 70 or carried a high-severity finding across the three pinned repositories, all six carry a hand-authored disposition, and two of the six were cost without value.
gates.why: Measured 0.333 (2 of 6) against a bar of 0.30. The widened corpus did not make this gate comfortable, it made it answerable: `e4.9`'s 60-episode pins gave a denominator of three and the gate had to refuse to read it (`not-measurable`, floor five). Now it has a denominator and it fails, narrowly. The wider sentence is unchanged and is next to it: `aggregate.cut_tau_alpha.flagged` is 6 in 540 episodes, so at the published τ the flag arm is carried almost entirely by high-severity findings and §5.4's α gate is a rate over a handful of episodes rather than over the population a reviewer is actually shown.

gates.claim: across every episode the corpus flagged — §5.4's default plus each repository's own top-decile cut, which is what a reviewer would actually have been shown — no more than 30 % of the labelled flags were cost without value
gates.why: Measured 0.697 on 66 labelled flags: 32 dismissed `low-stakes` (Dependabot, renovate and release-bot bumps, and `update dev dependencies` episodes that re-emit the CI workflow templates and a 500-to-1 600-line lockfile — the workflow and dependency axes raised them and no finding justified them), 9 `false-positive` (a test spy charged as untested new logic twice over, `# type: ignore` and `#[expect(deprecated)]` suppressions whose reason is written on the line above them, a `"TODO"` that is the name of a GitHub label, a fuzzer's own report charged as leftover debug output, and mdtest — ty's real test surface — counted as no tests at all twice), 5 `intentional` (a `gh repo garden` deletion that took its tests with it, three `test_weakening` skips that are platform and receipt guards, and dropping end-of-life Pythons). 26 of the 46 false positives were blamed on the ranking rather than on any detector — see `aggregate.coverage.blamed_on_score`. The finding is about where the flags come from, not only about the detectors, and tripling the corpus did not move it: 0.682 → 0.697.

gates.claim: the same population clears the 1.0 gate of 0.15
gates.why: 0.697 against 0.15. Written down so that the distance to the 1.0 gate is a measurement and not a vibe: closing it means the flag set stops being mostly routine dependency bumps, which is `e4.4`'s routing and `e4.3`'s catalogue together, not one of them alone.

gates.claim: at the published default tau, no more than 20 % of the episodes that later needed rework sat below the flag threshold
gates.why: Measured 1.000: all 24 mature reworked episodes in the corpus were below tau 70 — nothing in the 540 scored above 63, so the τ arm of §5.4's `F(τ,W)` did not fire anywhere in this corpus at all. This is the companion number §5.4 requires precisely because `G3` alone is satisfied by flagging nothing, and it is the number that says what the gate above cannot: on real OSS history the shipped score does not fire, so the guardrail's two halves fail in opposite directions and only `miss_rate` notices.

gates.claim: at each repository's own top-decile cut — the queue a reviewer would actually have read first — no more than 20 % of the reworked episodes were below it
gates.why: Measured 0.708 (17 of 24). Raising the threshold's strictness is not the same as raising its recall, and this is the number that shows it: even a cut that flags 66 of 540 episodes still misses most of the episodes that later needed rework, because what got reworked in these windows was ordinary-looking source edits, not lockfiles. This is also the gate the widened denominator was for: at 4 of 7 the difference between 0.20 and 0.60 was noise, and at 17 of 24 it is not.

gates.claim: the corpus contains at least 20 mature reworked episodes, which is what a 0.20 gate on a rate needs to be able to tell 0.20 from 0.60
gates.why: Measured 24 out of 525 mature episodes (4.6 %). `e4.9` declared this a `fail` about the corpus, not the product — rework is rare on a healthy repository, and 7 samples cannot discriminate a 0.20 gate — and the fix it named was a bigger pinned window rather than a relaxed threshold. Each pin now carries 180 episodes instead of 60 and `astral-sh/ruff` sits at a newer head, which is what clears the floor. Nothing in `thresholds.json`'s bars moved for this gate; the only other `expected` that changed in the same pass is `g3-alpha-at-published-tau`, and that moved because its denominator left the floor, not because anything improved.

gates.claim: every episode any cut flagged has a hand-authored disposition — a flag nobody labelled is a hole in the guardrail, and a guardrail with a hole in it is not a guardrail
gates.why: 66 flags, 66 labels, across all three cuts — 22 from the `e4.9` pass (every one of them still resolves inside the widened window and still sits on a flagged episode) and 44 written against the diff in the `reco-dyt` re-pin. No label was inferred from a score, a reason distribution or a template. `tests/test_g3_calibration_contract.py` also refuses a label with no note or no evidence, a reason code outside `e4.6`'s closed list, and a label keyed to a commit that is not in its pin's window.

gates.claim: the corpus flags at least 20 episodes, below which `G3` is a story about a handful of commits rather than a rate
gates.why: Measured 66 of 540 episodes — 26 `cli`, 20 `flask`, 20 `ruff`, which is the same 12 % flag share the 60-episode windows produced, so the cut is behaving like a rate and not like an accident of one quiet window. This gate exists so that a future re-pin to a quieter window fails loudly instead of turning every ratio gate into `not-measurable` and the suite into a green shrug.

gates.claim: no detector is disqualified by `e0.12`'s rule as this harness scores it: a default-enabled detector whose own false-positive rate breaches the alpha gate on at least 8 answerable flags (the bar a default flip has to clear, deliberately higher than the 5 a printed number has to clear) is a detector that must ship disabled. Read `why` before reading the 0 as a clean bill of health.
gates.why: Measured 0, and the 0 has a mechanism a reader has to know about: `defaults.breaches` asks each detector's *pooled* `g3`, and the pooling step never fills that field — per-repository rates are computed, the aggregate's are not — so every detector that spoke lands in `defaults.under_measured` (its message says "under the 8 a default flip needs" even at 13 flags, which is the tell) and the breach count is structurally zero. Scored instead against `aggregate.detectors_corpus`, which recomputes the rate from the pooled offenders and denominators, the widened corpus does now see three default-enabled detectors over α with at least 8 answerable flags: `lint_escape` 0.667 on 9, `untested_new_logic` 0.500 on 8, `test_weakening` 0.385 on 13. This harness therefore still flips no shipped default in either direction — `e4.3`'s four disabled detectors stay disabled, and `shotgun_edit`, the only disabled detector with a real denominator, measures 0.444 on 9 and does not earn re-enabling — but "which of those three does `e0.12`'s rule disqualify now" is a measurable question with an unanswered answer, and it belongs to its own ticket with the weights and the catalogue in it, not to a threshold edit here. `scope_creep`, `secret_string`, `churn_loop` and `rework_loop` still never fired in the corpus, which is no evidence rather than clean (`aggregate.defaults.never_fired` says which).

how_gates_are_set: Every gate declares `expected`: `pass`, `fail` or `not-measurable`. A gate that surprises us in either direction fails the run, because a claim that quietly starts passing has to be re-read just as hard as one that fails. The `fail` gates are the measurement's findings, not its defects: on three real OSS repositories — three windows of 180 episodes each, 540 episodes, 525 of them mature — the shipped score reaches §5.4's published default on six episodes and every one of the 24 episodes that were mature and later needed rework sat below the threshold, so the miss rate is 1.0; the same corpus measured at each repository's own top-decile cut puts 66 flags in front of a reviewer of which 46 were cost without value, and the α gate measures 0.333 on six labelled flags. Those are the numbers `e0.12`'s thresholds have to survive; they are written here rather than smoothed into a sentence. A gate is never adjusted to fit a measurement: the `min_denominator` floor is what turns an anecdote into `not-measurable` instead of into a comfortable `pass`, and when a gate's `expected` changed in the `reco-dyt` re-pin it changed because the gate started measuring something (`miss-rate-denominator-is-big-enough`, 7 → 24, and `g3-alpha-at-published-tau`, a denominator of 3 → 6), not because a bar moved.
